newsitem.title: KENYA: EU idea of African force for Zaire looks doomed.
newsitem.headline: EU idea of African force for Zaire looks doomed.

text.p: Despite appeals from Europe, there appears to be no chance of a pan-African military intervention in eastern Zaire's war zone, diplomats and analysts said on Friday.

The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) has kept silent about the European Union (EU) proposal on Wednesday that African troops should go in after a ceasefire and protect one million Rwandan refugees.
The idea smacks of buck-passing and the OAU has neither the resources nor the desire to quickly send in a military force with a quasi-humanitarian mission, African experts said.
"I don't see very much that Africa could do at this stage. I think we have to allow the situation to settle," said Bethwell Kiplagat, a leading Kenyan analyst of African affairs.

A bewildering mix of armed groups are fighting in eastern Zaire. They include the Zairean army, ethnic Tutsi rebels called the Banyamulenge, Rwanda's former Hutu government army and its Hutu militia, as well as indigenous Zaireans battling to keep control of their ancestral lands.
To add to the combustible cocktail, Rwanda's current army, which is overwhelmingly Tutsi, was engaged on Friday in serious cross-border artillery exchanges started by the Zairean army.
If there are any foreign volunteers offering to fly into that maelstrom to restore order, they do not include the OAU.
"I am not aware of any OAU response to the EU appeal," a senior African diplomat in Addis Ababa, site of the OAU headquarters, told Reuters.
"Not only would you need a ceasefire but the OAU does not have the capacity to mobilise a force at short notice and enter the theatre of conflict," he said.
The OAU and its secretary-general, Salim Ahmed Salim, have moved over the past three years to strengthen the 54-nation body's role in preventing and controlling the endless rash of African conflicts.
Western countries eager to disengage from Africa have helped finance the OAU's new conflict management division.
Yet despite outline plans for an African but western-funded force to end tribal slaughter in Burundi, there has been no deployment.
This is partly for strategic reasons -- Africans are wary the developed countries dominating the United Nations want to leave them solely responsible for the continent's conflicts.
A political consensus among OAU members, to send troops into Zaire, would be almost impossible because of deep disagreements about causes and solutions, diplomats say.
But nor do the OAU and the armies of its member states have the resources to deploy and supply the powerful force needed.
Salim chaired a session on Zaire of the OAU's conflict experts in Addis on Thursday.
A communique later was punctuated with phrases like "grave concern", "immediate cessation of hostilities" and "peaceful solution".

There was not the shadow of a suggestion the OAU was considering military options. Hopes are being pinned instead on a mini-African summit in Nairobi on Novemver 5, the same day EU ministers meet in Dublin to try to breathe life into their plan for an OAU force.
"It will be very, very difficult to send an OAU force in such a situation. Things are going too fast in Zaire and nobody understands where it's going," one African ambassador in Nairobi said.
The only African army with the capacity to intervene is South Africa's, but the politicians and generals there are not biting.
General George Meiring, chief of the South African Defence Force, said this week his partially integrated post-apartheid army would not be fully ready for peacekeeping in Africa until around 1999.
"Many of our troops are either tied up in training, giving training or assisting the police," he said.
